title: Parking permit
context: Listen to a conversation between a student and an employee at the campus parking office.

lines.t: Hi, I'd like to buy a parking permit for the spring semester.
Sure. Are you a commuter, or do you live in campus housing?
I commute. I live about forty minutes away, so I drive in three days a week.
In that case, you might not need a full permit. We have a part-time pass that covers up to three days a week, and it's about half the price.
Really? Nobody mentioned that at orientation. Can I park in Lot C with it? That's right next to the engineering building.
Unfortunately, no. The part-time pass is only valid in the north garage. It's about a ten-minute walk from engineering.
Ten minutes is nothing if I'm saving that much. I'll take the part-time pass.

options: Moving into campus housing
Parking in Lot C next to the engineering building
A cheaper pass for people who drive in only some days
Taking the bus three days a week
optionNotes: She only asks whether he lives on campus.
The part-time pass is not valid in Lot C.
Correct: she offers the part-time pass.
The bus is never mentioned.
questions.explanation: Because he drives in only three days a week, she suggests the part-time pass at about half the price.
questions.evidence: We have a part-time pass that covers up to three days a week

questions.prompt: What can be inferred about the man's decision?
options: He thinks the savings are worth a longer walk.
He is disappointed that he cannot park in the north garage.
He plans to drive to campus every day.
He learned about the pass at orientation.
optionNotes: Correct: 'Ten minutes is nothing' compared with the money saved.
He can park in the north garage; it is Lot C he cannot use.
He drives three days a week.
He says nobody mentioned it at orientation.
questions.explanation: He accepts the ten-minute walk because the pass is much cheaper.
questions.evidence: Ten minutes is nothing if I'm saving that much.

title: Choosing an arts elective
context: Listen to a conversation between two students.

lines.t: Have you picked your arts elective yet? Registration closes tomorrow.
I was going to take Introduction to Photography, but it turns out you need your own camera. A decent one costs more than my rent.
Ouch. What about the film studies course? I took it last year. You mostly watch classic movies and write short reviews.
That sounds more like my thing, honestly. Is the professor strict?
She's demanding about deadlines, but if you hand things in on time, she's really generous with grades.
Okay, I'm sold. I'll sign up tonight before I change my mind.

He took a similar course last year.
The equipment it requires is too expensive.

Strictness is discussed for the film course.

Not mentioned.
Movies are part of the course, not a plan.
questions.explanation: 'I'm sold' means I'm convinced; he will sign up for film studies.

title: Research assistant offer
context: Listen to a conversation between a student and a professor.

lines.t: Marcus, thanks for coming by. I wanted to ask whether you'd be interested in working in my lab next term. One of my research assistants is graduating.
Wow, I'm flattered. What would the job involve?
Mostly coding interview transcripts, about ten hours a week. It's tedious at times, I won't pretend otherwise, but you'd get your name on the paper if it's published.
That's a big deal for grad school applications. The only thing is, I've already promised the campus bookstore I'd work there next term.
Well, you'd hardly be the first student to juggle two jobs, but I'd rather you didn't burn out. Why not talk to the bookstore and see if they'd cut your hours?
That's fair. My manager's pretty flexible. I'll stop by the store this afternoon and let you know by Friday.

questions.prompt: What is the professor's attitude toward the research work?
options: She admits it can be dull but believes it offers a real benefit.
She thinks it is too difficult for an undergraduate.
She considers it less important than the bookstore job.
She is worried that the paper will not be published.
optionNotes: Correct: tedious, but his name would appear on the paper.
She never says it is difficult.
She wants him to reduce bookstore hours, not the research.
She says 'if it's published', but expresses no worry.
questions.explanation: She is honest that the work is tedious, but stresses the benefit of authorship.
questions.evidence: It's tedious at times, I won't pretend otherwise, but you'd get your name on the paper

questions.prompt: What will the man probably do next?
options: Turn down the research position

Ask his manager about working fewer hours
Start coding interview transcripts
optionNotes: He seems keen on the position.
He will ask about cutting hours, not quit.
Correct: he will visit the store as the professor suggested.
The job begins next term.
questions.explanation: The professor suggests asking the bookstore to cut his hours, and he agrees to go there this afternoon.
questions.evidence: I'll stop by the store this afternoon and let you know by Friday.

title: Tutoring schedule
context: Listen to a conversation between a student and the coordinator of the tutoring center.

lines.t: Hi, I signed up for chemistry tutoring, but the only session I was given is Friday at eight in the morning.
Ah, yes. Chemistry is our busiest subject, so the good times go fast.
The problem is, I work a night shift on Thursdays. I don't get home until two.

I see. Well, there's a waiting list for afternoon slots, and people drop out fairly often in the first few weeks. Or you could join a small group session on Monday evenings. It's three or four students with one tutor.
A group might actually be good. I'd hear other people's questions too.
Great. I'll move you to the Monday group and put your name on the waiting list just in case.

title: Poster session data
context: Listen to a conversation between a student and a professor.

lines.t: Professor Kessler, do you have a minute? It's about the student research poster session.
Of course. Your poster draft is due Monday, isn't it?
That's the thing. My survey closed late because so few people responded at first, so I've only just started analysing the data. I was wondering if I could present preliminary results instead.

Hmm. Preliminary results aren't ideal, but they're hardly unusual. Plenty of posters at real conferences are works in progress. What I'd want to see is a clear explanation of what you expect to find and why.
So I should focus more on my hypotheses than on conclusions.
Exactly. And frankly, being honest about a low response rate will impress the judges more than pretending your data is complete.

questions.prompt: What is the professor's attitude toward presenting preliminary results?
options: He thinks the judges will reject it.
He accepts it, as long as the student explains her expectations clearly.
He prefers that she wait until next year.
He believes only first-year students do it.
optionNotes: He says honesty will impress the judges.
Correct: not ideal, but hardly unusual.
Not suggested.
He says conference posters are often works in progress.
questions.explanation: 'Not ideal, but hardly unusual' shows acceptance with a condition: explain what she expects to find.
questions.evidence: Preliminary results aren't ideal, but they're hardly unusual.

questions.prompt: What does the professor suggest about the low response rate?
options: The student should collect more responses before Monday.
The judges will probably not notice it.
It shows her survey questions were badly written.
The student should mention it openly.
optionNotes: Not suggested.
He says honesty is better than pretending.
He never criticizes the questions.
Correct: honesty will impress the judges.
questions.explanation: He advises her to be honest about the response rate rather than hiding it.
questions.evidence: being honest about a low response rate will impress the judges more than pretending your data is complete
